Households

In this section, we describe what is arguably the most important economic agent in the OG-Core model: the household. We model households in OG-Core rather than individuals, because we want to abstract from the concepts of gender, marital status, and number of children. Furthermore, the household is the usual unit of account in tax data. Because OG-Core is primarily a fiscal policy model, it is advantageous to have the most granular unit of account be the household.

Household Consumption¶

We describe the derivation and dynamics of the population distribution in the Demographics chapter in this documentation and in more detail in the calibration chapter on demographics in the country-specific repository documentation. A measure ω1,t\omega_{1,t}ω1,t​ of households is born each period, become economically relevant at age s=E+1s=E+1s=E+1 if they survive to that age, and live for up to E+SE+SE+S periods (SSS economically active periods), with the population of age-sss individuals in period ttt being ωs,t\omega_{s,t}ωs,t​. Let the age of a household be indexed by s={1,2,...E+S}s = \{1,2,...E+S\}s={1,2,...E+S}.

At birth, each household age s=1s=1s=1 is randomly assigned one of JJJ ability groups, indexed by jjj. Let λj\lambda_jλj​ represent the fraction of individuals in each ability group, such that ∑jλj=1\sum_j\lambda_j=1∑j​λj​=1. Note that this implies that the distribution across ability types in each age is given by λ=[λ1,λ2,...λJ]\boldsymbol{\lambda}=[\lambda_1,\lambda_2,...\lambda_J]λ=[λ1​,λ2​,...λJ​]. Once an household is born and assigned to an ability type, it remains that ability type for its entire lifetime. This is deterministic ability heterogeneity as described in the calibration chapter on the lifetime earnings process in the country-specific repository documentation. Let ej,s>0e_{j,s}>0ej,s​>0 be a matrix of ability-levels such that an individual of ability type jjj will have lifetime abilities of [ej,1,ej,2,...ej,E+S][e_{j,1},e_{j,2},...e_{j,E+S}][ej,1​,ej,2​,...ej,E+S​].

Individuals in this economy choose how much to work each period nj,s,tn_{j,s,t}nj,s,t​ and how much to consume among III different consumption goods ci,j,s,tc_{i,j,s,t}ci,j,s,t​. We assume that households aggregate these industry-specific consumption goods in their preferences into a composite consumption good cj,s,tc_{j,s,t}cj,s,t​ every period in every individual’s preferences according to the following Stone-Geary version of a Cobb-Douglas consumption aggregator,

where cmin,ic_{min,i}cmin,i​ is the minimum consumption of good iii allowed.[1]

Assume that the non-normalized price of each individual consumption good is p~i,t\tilde{p}_{i,t}p~​i,t​. We can solve for the optimal good-iii consumption demands ci,j,s,tc_{i,j,s,t}ci,j,s,t​ as a function of composite consumption cj,s,tc_{j,s,t}cj,s,t​ by minimizing the total after-tax expenditure on consumption given that individual consumption adds up to composite consumption according to (14). Letting τi,tc\tau^{c}_{i,t}τi,tc​ represent the consumption tax rate on goods of type iii, the Lagrangian for this expenditure minimization problem is the following.

Budget Constraint¶

Because the household’s industry-specific demand problem from Section Household Consumption is characterized by equations (14), (23), and (24) is determined by functions of composite consumption cj,s,tc_{j,s,t}cj,s,t​ and normalized industry prices ptp_tpt​ and pi,tp_{i,t}pi,t​, we can write the individual’s utility maximization in terms of composite consumption cj,s,tc_{j,s,t}cj,s,t​. An ability-jjj and age-sss individual faces the following per-period budget constraint.

ptcj,s,t+∑i=1I(1+τi,tc)pi,tcmin,i+bj,s+1,t+1=(1+rp,t)bj,s,t+wtej,snj,s,t...+(1−τtbq)bqj,s,t+rmj,s,t+trj,s,t+ubij,s,t+pensionj,s,t−taxj,s,t∀j,tandE+1≤s≤E+Swherebj,E+1,t=0\begin{aligned} p_t c_{j,s,t} + &\sum_{i=1}^I (1 + \tau^{c}_{i,t})p_{i,t}c_{min,i} + b_{j,s+1,t+1} = \\ &(1 + r_{p,t})b_{j,s,t} + w_t e_{j,s} n_{j,s,t} ... \\ &\quad\quad + (1-\tau^{bq}_t)bq_{j,s,t} + rm_{j,s,t} + tr_{j,s,t} + ubi_{j,s,t} + pension_{j,s,t} - tax_{j,s,t} \\ &\quad\quad\forall j,t\quad\text{and}\quad E+1\leq s\leq E+S \quad\text{where}\quad b_{j,E+1,t}=0 \end{aligned}pt​cj,s,t​+​i=1∑I​(1+τi,tc​)pi,t​cmin,i​+bj,s+1,t+1​=(1+rp,t​)bj,s,t​+wt​ej,s​nj,s,t​...+(1−τtbq​)bqj,s,t​+rmj,s,t​+trj,s,t​+ubij,s,t​+pensionj,s,t​−taxj,s,t​∀j,tandE+1≤s≤E+Swherebj,E+1,t​=0​
(26)

where cj,s,tc_{j,s,t}cj,s,t​ is consumption, bj,s+1,t+1b_{j,s+1,t+1}bj,s+1,t+1​ is savings for the next period, rp,tr_{p,t}rp,t​ is the normalized interest rate (return) on household savings invested in the financial intermediary, bj,s,tb_{j,s,t}bj,s,t​ is current period wealth (savings from last period), wtw_twt​ is the normalized wage, and nj,s,tn_{j,s,t}nj,s,t​ is labor supply. Equations (123) and (124) of Chapter Financial Intermediary show how the rate of return from the financial intermediary rp,tr_{p,t}rp,t​ might differ from the marginal product of capital rtr_trt​ and from the interest rate the government pays rgov,tr_{gov,t}rgov,t​. Note that we must add in the cost of minimum consumption cmin,ic_{min,i}cmin,i​ for all iii because that amount is subtracted out of composite consumption in (14).

The last six terms on the right-hand-side of the budget constraint (26) have to do with dfferent types of transfers to households: bequests bqj,s,tbq_{j,s,t}bqj,s,t​, remittances rmj,s,trm_{j,s,t}rmj,s,t​, government transfers trj,s,ttr_{j,s,t}trj,s,t​, universal basic income ubij,s,tubi_{j,s,t}ubij,s,t​, public pension benefits pensionj,s,tpension_{j,s,t}pensionj,s,t​, and net taxes taxj,s,ttax_{j,s,t}taxj,s,t​. The first four types of transfers to households are detailed in the section below entitled Transfers to household.

The third term bqj,s,tbq_{j,s,t}bqj,s,t​ on the right-hand-side of the budget constraint (26) represents the portion of total bequests BQtBQ_tBQt​ that go to the age-sss, income-group-jjj household. Section Bequests details how total bequests are distributed among the different households. The next term on the right-hand-side of the budget constraint (26) represents remittances received by the household rmj,s,trm_{j,s,t}rmj,s,t​. We describe these remittances in Section Remittances below.

The next term is government transfers trj,s,ttr_{j,s,t}trj,s,t​ to households of lifetime income group jjj in age sss at time ttt. Section Government transfers details how total government transfers to households are distributed among the differenty household types. The term ubij,s,tubi_{j,s,t}ubij,s,t​ the time series of a matrix of universal basic income (UBI) transfers by lifetime income group jjj and age group sss in each period ttt. There is a specification where the time series of this matrix is stationary (growth adjusted) and a specification in which it’s stationary value is going to zero in the limit (non-growth-adjusted). The calibration chapter on UBI in the country-specific repository documentation describes the exact way in which this matrix is calibrated from the values of five parameters, household composition data, and OG-Core’s demographics. Similar to the transfers term TRtTR_{t}TRt​, the UBI transfers will not be distortionary.

Government pension systems are modeled explicitly and enter the budget through the pensionj,s,tpension_{j,s,t}pensionj,s,t​ term. The rules and parameters of the available public pension rules and parameters are in the Pensions section of chapter Government. The term taxj,s,ttax_{j,s,t}taxj,s,t​ is the total tax liability of the household in terms of the numeraire good. This term can include means tested benefit programs. In contrast to government transfers trj,s,ttr_{j,s,t}trj,s,t​, tax liability can be a function of labor income (xj,s,t≡wtej,snj,s,t)(x_{j,s,t}\equiv w_t e_{j,s}n_{j,s,t})(xj,s,t​≡wt​ej,s​nj,s,t​) and capital income (yj,s,t≡rp,tbj,s,t)(y_{j,s,t}\equiv r_{p,t} b_{j,s,t})(yj,s,t​≡rp,t​bj,s,t​) and wealth, bj,s,tb_{j,s,t}bj,s,t​. The tax liability can, therefore, be a distortionary influence on household decisions. It becomes valuable to represent total tax liability as the sum of an effective income tax rate τs,tetr,xy\tau^{etr,xy}_{s,t}τs,tetr,xy​ function multiplied by total income plus an effective tax rate on wealth τs,tetr,w\tau^{etr,w}_{s,t}τs,tetr,w​ multiplied by wealth,

taxj,s,t=τs,tetr,xy(xj,s,t,yj,s,t)(xj,s,t+yj,s,t)+τs,tetr,w(bj,s,t)bj,s,t∀j,s,t tax_{j,s,t} = \tau^{etr,xy}_{s,t}(x_{j,s,t}, y_{j,s,t})\left(x_{j,s,t} + y_{j,s,t}\right) + \tau^{etr,w}_{s,t}\left(b_{j,s,t}\right)b_{j,s,t} \quad\forall j,s,ttaxj,s,t​=τs,tetr,xy​(xj,s,t​,yj,s,t​)(xj,s,t​+yj,s,t​)+τs,tetr,w​(bj,s,t​)bj,s,t​∀j,s,t
(27)

where the effective income tax rate on labor and capital income can be a function of both labor income and capital income, respectively, τs,tetr,xy(xj,s,t,yj,s,t)\tau^{etr,xy}_{s,t}(x_{j,s,t},y_{j,s,t})τs,tetr,xy​(xj,s,t​,yj,s,t​), and the effective tax rate on wealth is given by the functional form described in Section Wealth taxes. The calibration chapter on the microsimulation model and tax function estimation in the country-specific repository documentation details exactly how the model estimates the income tax functions from microsimulation model data.

Elliptical Disutility of Labor Supply¶

In OG-Core, the period utility function of each household is a function of consumption cj,s,tc_{j,s,t}cj,s,t​, savings bj,s+1,t+1b_{j,s+1,t+1}bj,s+1,t+1​, and labor supply nj,s,tn_{j,s,t}nj,s,t​.[4] We detail this utility function, its justification, and functional form in Section Optimality Conditions. With endogenous labor supply nj,s,tn_{j,s,t}nj,s,t​, we must specify how labor enters an agent’s utility function and what are the constraints. Assume that each household is endowed with a measure of time l~\tilde{l}l~ each period that it can choose to spend as either labor nj,s,t∈[0,l~]n_{j,s,t}\in[0,\tilde{l}]nj,s,t​∈[0,l~] or leisure lj,s,t∈[0,l~]l_{j,s,t}\in[0,\tilde{l}]lj,s,t​∈[0,l~].

nj,s,t+lj,s,t=l~∀s,tn_{j,s,t} + l_{j,s,t} = \tilde{l} \quad\forall s, tnj,s,t​+lj,s,t​=l~∀s,t
(28)

The functional form for the utility of leisure or the disutility of labor supply has important implications for the computational tractability of the model. One difference of the household’s labor supply decision nj,s,tn_{j,s,t}nj,s,t​ from the consumption decision cj,s,tc_{j,s,t}cj,s,t​ is that the consumption decision only has a lower bound cj,s,t≥0c_{j,s,t}\geq 0cj,s,t​≥0 whereas the labor supply decision has both upper and lower bounds nj,s,t∈[0,l~]n_{j,s,t}\in[0,\tilde{l}]nj,s,t​∈[0,l~]. Evans & Phillips (2017) show that many of the traditional functional forms for the disutility of labor---Cobb-Douglas, constant Frisch elasticty, constant relative risk aversion (CRRA)---do not have Inada conditions on both the upper and lower bounds of labor supply. To solve these in a heterogeneous agent model would require occasionally binding constraints, which is a notoriously difficult computational problem.

Source
import ogcore.parameter_plots as pp
from ogcore import Specifications
p = Specifications()
p.update_specifications({'frisch': 0.6})
fig = pp.plot_elliptical_u(p)

Evans & Phillips (2017) propose using an equation for an ellipse to match the disutility of labor supply to whatever traditional functional form one wants. Our preferred specification in OG-Core is to fit an elliptical disutility of labor supply function to approximate a linearly separable constant Frisch elasticity (CFE) functional form. Let v(n)v(n)v(n) be a general disutility of labor function. A CFE disutility of labor function is the following,

v(n)≡n1+1θ1+1θ,θ>0v(n) \equiv \frac{n^{1+\frac{1}{\theta}}}{1+\frac{1}{\theta}}, \quad\theta > 0v(n)≡1+θ1​n1+θ1​​,θ>0
(29)

where θ>0\theta>0θ>0 represents the Frisch elasticity of labor supply. The elliptical disutility of labor supply functional form is the following,

v(n)=−b[1−(nl~)υ]1υ,b,υ>0v(n) = -b\left[1 - \left(\frac{n}{\tilde{l}}\right)^\upsilon\right]^{\frac{1}{\upsilon}}, \quad b,\upsilon>0v(n)=−b[1−(l~n​)υ]υ1​,b,υ>0
(30)

where b>0b>0b>0 is a scale parameter and υ>0\upsilon>0υ>0 is a curvature parameter. This functional form satisfies both v′(n)>0v'(n)>0v′(n)>0 and v′′(n)>0v''(n)>0v′′(n)>0 for all n∈(0,1)n\in(0,1)n∈(0,1). Further, it has Inada conditions at both the upper and lower bounds of labor supply lim⁡n→0v′(n)=0\lim_{n\rightarrow 0}v'(n) = 0limn→0​v′(n)=0 and lim⁡n→l~v′(n)=−∞\lim_{n\rightarrow \tilde{l}}v'(n) = -\inftylimn→l~​v′(n)=−∞.

Because it is the marginal disutility of labor supply that matters for household decision making, we want to choose the parameters of the elliptical disutility of labor supply function (b,υ)(b,\upsilon)(b,υ) so that the elliptical marginal utilities match the marginal utilities of the CFE disutility of labor supply. Figure Figure 1 shows the fit of marginal utilities for a Frisch elasticity of θ=0.9\theta=0.9θ=0.9 and a total time endowment of l~=1.0\tilde{l}=1.0l~=1.0. The estimated elliptical utility parameters in this case are b=0.527b=0.527b=0.527 and υ=1.497\upsilon=1.497υ=1.497.[5]

Transfers to household¶

The household budget constraint (26) includes four terms that represent different types of transfers to households: bequests bqj,s,tbq_{j,s,t}bqj,s,t​, remittances rmj,s,trm_{j,s,t}rmj,s,t​, government transfers trj,s,ttr_{j,s,t}trj,s,t​, and universal basic income ubij,s,tubi_{j,s,t}ubij,s,t​. These four types of household transfers are detailed in the following subsections.

Bequests¶

OG-Core allows for two parameterizations of the distribution of bequests. Users can choose the bequest transmission process through two parameters: use_zeta and zeta.

If use_zeta=False, then bequests from households of lifetime earnings type j are distributed equally across households of type j,

bqj,s,t=BQj,tλjωs,t bq_{j,s,t} = \frac{BQ_{j,t}}{\lambda_j \omega_{s,t}}bqj,s,t​=λj​ωs,t​BQj,t​​
(31)

where BQj,tBQ_{j,t}BQj,t​ is the total amount of bequests from the deceased in lifetime income group jjj. Note that the sum of all the BQj,tBQ_{j,t}BQj,t​ equals aggregate bequests BQtBQ_tBQt​ from equation (138).

BQj,t≡(1+rp,t)λj(∑s=E+2E+S+1ρs−1ωs−1,t−1bj,s,t)∀j,t BQ_{j,t} \equiv (1+r_{p,t})\lambda_j\left(\sum_{s=E+2}^{E+S+1}\rho_{s-1}\omega_{s-1,t-1}b_{j,s,t}\right) \quad\forall j,tBQj,t​≡(1+rp,t​)λj​(s=E+2∑E+S+1​ρs−1​ωs−1,t−1​bj,s,t​)∀j,t
(32)

If use_zeta=True, then in the distribution of bequests across age and lifetime ability is determined by ζj,s,t\zeta_{j,s,t}ζj,s,t​, which allocates aggregate bequests across households by age and lifetime income group:

Let ζj,s,t\zeta_{j,s,t}ζj,s,t​ be the fraction of total bequests BQtBQ_tBQt​ that go to the age-sss, income-group-jjj household, such that ∑s=E+1E+S∑j=1Jζj,s=1\sum_{s=E+1}^{E+S}\sum_{j=1}^J\zeta_{j,s}=1∑s=E+1E+S​∑j=1J​ζj,s​=1. We must divide that amount by the population of (j,s)(j,s)(j,s) households λjωs,t\lambda_j\omega_{s,t}λj​ωs,t​. The calibration chapter on beqests in the country-specific repository documentation details how to calibrate the ζj,s,t\zeta_{j,s,t}ζj,s,t​ values from consumer finance data.

Remittances¶

Remittances represent capital, most often currency balances, collected from ex patriots and citizens living abroad and sent back to households in the country. For most developed countries, like the United States, remittances represent an insignificant amount.[6] But for countries like the Phillipines, total incoming remittances are larger than total exports (?% of GDP in 202?).[7]

We calibrate remittances to initially be an exogenous fraction of GDP αRM,0\alpha_{RM,0}αRM,0​ but can grow from the initial period at a growth rate that differs from the endogenous growth rate of GDP and from the long-run growth rate of GDP (gy+gˉng_y + \bar{g}_ngy​+gˉ​n​).

RMt={αRM,1Ytfort=1,(1+gRM,t)RMt−1for2≤t≤TG1,(t−TG1TG2−TG1)αRM,TYt+(1−t−TG1TG2−TG1)(1+gRM,t)RMt−1  for  TG1<t<TG2,αRM,TYt∀t≥TG2RM_t = \begin{cases} &\alpha_{RM,1}Y_t \quad\text{for}\quad t=1, \\ &\left(1 + g_{RM,t}\right)RM_{t-1} \quad\text{for}\quad 2\leq t \leq T_{G1}, \\ &\left(\frac{t - T_{G1}}{T_{G2} - T_{G1}}\right)\alpha_{RM,T}Y_t + \left(1 - \frac{t - T_{G1}}{T_{G2} - T_{G1}}\right)\left(1 + g_{RM,t}\right)RM_{t-1} \:\:\text{for}\:\: T_{G1} < t < T_{G2}, \\ &\alpha_{RM,T}Y_t \quad\forall t\geq T_{G2} \end{cases}RMt​=⎩⎨⎧​​αRM,1​Yt​fort=1,(1+gRM,t​)RMt−1​for2≤t≤TG1​,(TG2​−TG1​t−TG1​​)αRM,T​Yt​+(1−TG2​−TG1​t−TG1​​)(1+gRM,t​)RMt−1​forTG1​<t<TG2​,αRM,T​Yt​∀t≥TG2​​
(34)

The first two lines of (34) represent the transition path of remittances before the closure rule, which are growing at a rate independent of the growth rate of the country economy. But for the steady-state to exists, total remittances must grow at the long-run growth rate of GDP before reaching the steady state. Similar to the closure rule’s described in Section Budget Closure Rule of Chapter Government, we implement a stabilizing rule that gradually transitions the growth rate of aggregate remittances from its exogenous rate through period TG1T_{G1}TG1​ to the long run economic growth rate after period TG2T_{G2}TG2​.

It is important to note that we specify the growth rate of remittances on nominal GPD as an initial percent αRM,1\alpha_{RM,1}αRM,1​, a growth rate based on those initial remittances, then a movemnt back to a rate relative to nominal GDP. This will result in stationary equations in which it matters wither the growth rate of nominal GDP gRM,tg_{RM,t}gRM,t​ is greater or less than the growth rate of labor productivity plus the population growth rate egy(1+gn,t)e^{g_y}\left(1+g_{n,t}\right)egy​(1+gn,t​). See equations (146) and (147) in Section Stationarized Household Equations in Chapter Stationarization.

The aggregate remittances RMtRM_tRMt​ are then distributed by the ηRM,j,s,t\eta_{RM,j,s,t}ηRM,j,s,t​ matrix, resulting in the value on the income side of the household budget constraint in (26).

rmj,s,t=ηRM,j,s,tRMtλjωs,t∀j,s,trm_{j,s,t} = \eta_{RM,j,s,t}\frac{RM_t}{\lambda_j\omega_{s,t}} \quad\forall \quad j,s,trmj,s,t​=ηRM,j,s,t​λj​ωs,t​RMt​​∀j,s,t
(35)

The distribution object ηRM,j,s,t\eta_{RM,j,s,t}ηRM,j,s,t​ is an S×JS\times JS×J matrix in every period ttt whose elements sum to one in every period. This object governs how total remittances in every period RMtRM_tRMt​ are distributed as income among household budget constraints.

Government transfers¶

Section Lump sum transfers: in chapter Government details how aggregate government transfers to households TRtTR_{t}TRt​ in every period are a percentage of total GDP. We assume here that each household’s portion of those tranfers in every period can be calibrated using the matrix of percentages ηj,s,t\eta_{j,s,t}ηj,s,t​ in every time period to allocate the transfers by a household’s lifetime income group jjj and age sss. Then the ηj,s,t\eta_{j,s,t}ηj,s,t​ allocation percentages can also vary over time ttt.

trj,s,t=ηj,s,tTRtλjωs,t∀j,t,andE+1≤s≤E+S tr_{j,s,t} = \eta_{j,s,t}\frac{TR_{t}}{\lambda_j \omega_{s,t}} \forall j,t, \quad\text{and}\quad E+1\leq s\leq E+Strj,s,t​=ηj,s,t​λj​ωs,t​TRt​​∀j,t,andE+1≤s≤E+S
(36)

These transfers to household are lump sum and only influence households’ decisions through how they change income in the budget constraint. These transfers do not include pension payments or tax credits.

is total government transfers to households in period ttt and ηj,s,t\eta_{j,s,t}ηj,s,t​ is the percent of those transfers that go to households of age sss and lifetime income group jjj such that ∑s=E+1E+S∑j=1Jηj,s,t=1\sum_{s=E+1}^{E+S}\sum_{j=1}^J\eta_{j,s,t}=1∑s=E+1E+S​∑j=1J​ηj,s,t​=1. This term is divided by the population of type (j,s)(j,s)(j,s) households. We assume government transfers to be lump sum, so they do not create any direct distortions to household decisions. Total government transfers TRtTR_tTRt​ is in terms of the numeraire good, as shown in equation (93) in Chapter Government.

Optimality Conditions¶

Households choose lifetime consumption {cj,s,t+s−1}s=1S\{c_{j,s,t+s-1}\}_{s=1}^S{cj,s,t+s−1​}s=1S​, labor supply {nj,s,t+s−1}s=1S\{n_{j,s,t+s-1}\}_{s=1}^S{nj,s,t+s−1​}s=1S​, and savings {bj,s+1,t+s}s=1S\{b_{j,s+1,t+s}\}_{s=1}^{S}{bj,s+1,t+s​}s=1S​ to maximize lifetime utility, subject to the budget constraints and non negativity constraints. The household period utility function is the following.

u(cj,s,t,nj,s,t,bj,s+1,t+1)≡(cj,s,t)1−σ−11−σ+egyt(1−σ)χsn(b[1−(nj,s,tl~)υ]1υ)+χjbρs(bj,s+1,t+1)1−σ−11−σ∀j,tandE+1≤s≤E+S\begin{aligned} u(c_{j,s,t},n_{j,s,t},b_{j,s+1,t+1}) &\equiv \frac{(c_{j,s,t})^{1-\sigma} - 1}{1-\sigma} + e^{g_y t(1-\sigma)}\chi^n_s\biggl(b\left[1 - \left(\frac{n_{j,s,t}}{\tilde{l}}\right)^\upsilon\right]^{\frac{1}{\upsilon}}\biggr) + \\ &\chi^b_j \rho_s \frac{(b_{j,s+1,t+1})^{1-\sigma} - 1}{1-\sigma} \quad\forall j,t \quad\text{and}\quad E+1 \leq s \leq E+S \end{aligned}u(cj,s,t​,nj,s,t​,bj,s+1,t+1​)​≡1−σ(cj,s,t​)1−σ−1​+egy​t(1−σ)χsn​(b[1−(l~nj,s,t​​)υ]υ1​)+χjb​ρs​1−σ(bj,s+1,t+1​)1−σ−1​∀j,tandE+1≤s≤E+S​
(37)

The period utility function (37) is linearly separable in cj,s,tc_{j,s,t}cj,s,t​, nj,s,tn_{j,s,t}nj,s,t​, and bj,s+1,t+1b_{j,s+1,t+1}bj,s+1,t+1​. The first term is a constant relative risk aversion (CRRA) utility of consumption. The second term is the elliptical disutility of labor described in Section Elliptical Disutility of Labor Supply. The constant χsn\chi^n_sχsn​ adjusts the disutility of labor supply relative to consumption and can vary by age sss, which is helpful for calibrating the model to match labor market moments. See the chapters in the Calibration section of this documentation for a discussion of the calibration.

It is necessary to multiply the disutility of labor in (37) by egy(1−σ)e^{g_y(1-\sigma)}egy​(1−σ) because labor supply nj,s,tn_{j,s,t}nj,s,t​ is stationary, but both consumption cj,s,tc_{j,s,t}cj,s,t​ and savings bj,s+1,t+1b_{j,s+1,t+1}bj,s+1,t+1​ are growing at the rate of technological progress (see Chapter Stationarization). The egy(1−σ)e^{g_y(1-\sigma)}egy​(1−σ) term keeps the relative utility values of consumption, labor supply, and savings in the same units.

The final term in the period utility function (37) is the “warm glow” bequest motive. It is a CRRA utility of savings, discounted by the mortality rate ρs\rho_sρs​.[8] Intuitively, it signifies the utility a household gets in the event that they don’t live to the next period with probability ρs\rho_sρs​. It is a utility of savings beyond its usual benefit of allowing for more consumption in the next period. This utility of bequests also has constant χjb\chi^b_jχjb​ which adjusts the utility of bequests relative to consumption and can vary by lifetime income group jjj. This is helpful for calibrating the model to match wealth distribution moments. See the calibration chapter on beqests in the country-specific repository documentation for a discussion of the calibration. Note that any bequest before age E+SE+SE+S is unintentional as it was bequeathed due an event of death that was uncertain. Intentional bequests are all bequests given in the final period of life in which death is certain bj,E+S+1,tb_{j,E+S+1,t}bj,E+S+1,t​.

The household lifetime optimization problem is to choose consumption cj,s,tc_{j,s,t}cj,s,t​, labor supply nj,s,tn_{j,s,t}nj,s,t​, and savings bj,s+1,t+1b_{j,s+1,t+1}bj,s+1,t+1​ in every period of life to maximize expected discounted lifetime utility, subject to budget constraints and upper-bound and lower-bound constraints.

max⁡{(cj,s,t),(nj,s,t),(bj,s+1,t+1)}s=E+1E+S ∑s=1Sβjs−1[Πu=E+1E+s(1−ρu)]u(cj,s,t+s−1,nj,s,t+s−1,bj,s+1,t+s) \max_{\{(c_{j,s,t}),(n_{j,s,t}),(b_{j,s+1,t+1})\}_{s=E+1}^{E+S}}\: \sum_{s=1}^S\beta_j^{s-1}\left[\Pi_{u=E+1}^{E+s}(1 - \rho_u)\right]u(c_{j,s,t+s-1},n_{j,s,t+s-1},b_{j,s+1,t+s}){(cj,s,t​),(nj,s,t​),(bj,s+1,t+1​)}s=E+1E+S​max​s=1∑S​βjs−1​[Πu=E+1E+s​(1−ρu​)]u(cj,s,t+s−1​,nj,s,t+s−1​,bj,s+1,t+s​)
(38)
s.t.ptcj,s,t+∑i=1I(1+τi,tc)pi,tcmin,i+bj,s+1,t+1=(1+rp,t)bj,s,t+wtej,snj,s,t...+ (1−τtbq)bqj,s,t+rmj,s,t+trj,s,t+ubij,s,t+pensionj,s,t−taxj,s,tandcj,s,t≥0, nj,s,t∈[0,l~], and bj,1,t=0∀j,t, and E+1≤s≤E+S\begin{aligned} \text{s.t.}\quad &p_t c_{j,s,t} + \sum_{i=1}^I (1 + \tau^{c}_{i,t})p_{i,t}c_{min,i} + b_{j,s+1,t+1} = \\ &\quad (1 + r_{p,t})b_{j,s,t} + w_t e_{j,s} n_{j,s,t} ...\\ &\qquad +\: (1-\tau^{bq}_t)bq_{j,s,t} + rm_{j,s,t} + tr_{j,s,t} + ubi_{j,s,t} + pension_{j,s,t} - tax_{j,s,t} \\ &\qquad\text{and}\quad c_{j,s,t}\geq 0,\: n_{j,s,t} \in[0,\tilde{l}],\:\text{and}\: b_{j,1,t}=0 \quad\forall j, t, \:\text{and}\: E+1\leq s\leq E+S \end{aligned}s.t.​pt​cj,s,t​+i=1∑I​(1+τi,tc​)pi,t​cmin,i​+bj,s+1,t+1​=(1+rp,t​)bj,s,t​+wt​ej,s​nj,s,t​...+(1−τtbq​)bqj,s,t​+rmj,s,t​+trj,s,t​+ubij,s,t​+pensionj,s,t​−taxj,s,t​andcj,s,t​≥0,nj,s,t​∈[0,l~],andbj,1,t​=0∀j,t,andE+1≤s≤E+S​

The nonnegativity constraint on consumption does not bind in equilibrium because of the Inada condition lim⁡c→0u1(c,n,b′)=∞\lim_{c\rightarrow 0}u_1(c,n,b') = \inftylimc→0​u1​(c,n,b′)=∞, which implies consumption is always strictly positive in equilibrium cj,s,t>0c_{j,s,t}>0cj,s,t​>0 for all jjj, sss, and ttt. The warm glow bequest motive in Equation (37) also has an Inada condition for savings at zero, so bj,s,t>0b_{j,s,t}>0bj,s,t​>0 for all jjj, sss, and ttt. This is an implicit borrowing constraint.[9] And note that the discount factor βj\beta_jβj​ has a jjj subscript for lifetime income group. Factor Transforming Income Units¶

The tax functions τs,tetr,xy\tau^{etr,xy}_{s,t}τs,tetr,xy​, τs,tetr,w\tau^{etr,w}_{s,t}τs,tetr,w​, τs,tmtrx\tau^{mtrx}_{s,t}τs,tmtrx​, τs,tmtry\tau^{mtry}_{s,t}τs,tmtry​, and τs,tmtrw\tau^{mtrw}_{s,t}τs,tmtrw​ are estimated in each country calibration model based on the currency units of the corresponding income data. However, the consumption units of the OG-Core model or any of its country calibrations are not in the same units as income data. For this reason, we have to transform the model income units xxx and yyy by a factorfactorfactor so that they are in the same units as the income data on which the tax functions were estimated.

The tax rate functions are each functions of capital income and labor income τ(x,y)\tau(x,y)τ(x,y). In order to make the tax functions return accurate tax rates associated with the correct levels of income, we multiply the model income xIx^IxI and yIy^IyI by a factorfactorfactor so that they are in the same units as the real-world income data τ(factor×xI,factor×yI)\tau(factor\times x^I, factor\times y^I)τ(factor×xI,factor×yI). We define the factorfactorfactor such that average steady-state household total income in the model times the factorfactorfactor equals the U.S. data average total income.

factor×[∑s=E+1E+S∑j=1Jλjωˉs(wˉej,snˉj,s+rˉpbˉj,s)]=Avg. household inc. in data factor \times \Biggl[\sum_{s=E+1}^{E+S}\sum_{j=1}^J\lambda_j\bar{\omega}_s\left(\bar{w}e_{j,s}\bar{n}_{j,s} + \bar{r}_{p}\bar{b}_{j,s}\right)\Biggr] = \text{Avg. household inc. in data}factor×[s=E+1∑E+S​j=1∑J​λj​ωˉs​(wˉej,s​nˉj,s​+rˉp​bˉj,s​)]=Avg. household inc. in data
(43)

We do not know the steady-state wage, interest rate, household labor supply, and savings ex ante. So the income factorfactorfactor is an endogenous variable in the steady-state equilibrium computational solution. We hold the factor constant throughout the nonsteady-state equilibrium solution.

Expectations¶

To conclude the household’s problem, we must make an assumption about how the age-sss household can forecast the time path of interest rates paid by firms (marginal product of capital), wages, and total bequests {ru,wu,BQu}u=tt+S−s\{r_u, w_u, BQ_u\}_{u=t}^{t+S-s}{ru​,wu​,BQu​}u=tt+S−s​ over his remaining lifetime. As we will show in Chapter Equilibrium, the equilibrium interest rate paid by firms (marginal product of capital) rtr_trt​, wage wtw_twt​, and total bequests BQtBQ_tBQt​ will be functions of the state vector Γt\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_tΓt​, which turns out to be the entire distribution of savings in period ttt.

Define Γt\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_tΓt​ as the distribution of household savings across households at time ttt.

Γt≡{bj,s,t}s=E+2E+S∀j,t \boldsymbol{\Gamma}_t \equiv \bigl\{b_{j,s,t}\bigr\}_{s=E+2}^{E+S} \quad\forall j,tΓt​≡{bj,s,t​}s=E+2E+S​∀j,t
(44)

Let general beliefs about the future distribution of capital in period t+ut+ut+u be characterized by the operator Ω(⋅)\Omega(\cdot)Ω(⋅) such that:

Γt+ue=Ωu(Γt)∀t,u≥1 \boldsymbol{\Gamma}^e_{t+u} = \Omega^u\left(\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_t\right) \quad \forall t, \quad u\geq 1Γt+ue​=Ωu(Γt​)∀t,u≥1
(45)

where the eee superscript signifies that Γt+ue\boldsymbol{\Gamma}^e_{t+u}Γt+ue​ is the expected distribution of wealth at time t+ut+ut+u based on general beliefs Ω(⋅)\Omega(\cdot)Ω(⋅) that are not constrained to be correct. [10]
